question: How should dimensional models represent voyages and routes (trips with legs, segments and stops), and how should dates, times and time zones be handled in them?
contributions: Fact tables at different levels of granularity (leg, segment, trip, itinerary)
Combining role-playing dimensions into a superdimension in certain situations
Time of day as a fact versus dimension
Dates and times in multiple time zones

limits: Design guidance from the authors' experience; no measurements, benchmarks or empirical comparison of alternatives.
Published 2002: Web-site sales channel, toll-free phone and similar examples are dated, and no columnar or cloud warehouse considerations appear.
Authors concede country-specific calendars are messy and worse with local holidays that differ within a country.
Combining dimensions is stated to be the exception rather than the rule.
practices: Choose the grain by business process and begin at the lowest grain with meaningful metrics (segment, here), not the most granular leg data (p.231).
Keep the fact table at segment grain and add trip origin and trip destination as extra role-playing airport dimensions to answer where flyers are going (p.233).
Build a trip-grain aggregate table only if segment-level rollups show obvious performance or usability problems (p.234).
Take care summarizing at trip level in a segment-grain table, since fare basis and class of service do not apply at trip level (p.233).
Implement role-playing dimensions as separate logical views on a single physical table (date, time, airport) (p.231, p.238).
Split volatile or analytic attributes (elite tier, home airport, club membership) into a frequent flyer profile minidimension (p.232).
Do not separate promotion from fare basis when business users treat them as inextricably linked (p.232).
Combine role-playing dimensions into a superdimension only when row counts are extremely small or attributes depend on the combination (class of service, city-pair) (p.238).
Put standardised city-pair labels (e.g. SFO-DEN) in a dimension table rather than in application code (p.237).
If row counts prohibit a combined origin/destination dimension, keep separate dimensions and add a third city-pair dimension to the fact table (p.238).
Model multinational calendars as a primary date dimension plus a country-specific outrigger keyed on date key and country (p.239).

Keep time of day out of the date dimension to avoid a row explosion; use a time-of-day dimension when grouping (15-minute, hour, AM/PM, rush period) is needed, otherwise a numeric fact of minutes or seconds since midnight (p.240).
For multiple time zones carry both local and equalized (GMT or headquarters) date and time-of-day, as separate dimensions or time-of-day facts (p.241).
Cargo schemas: make the bill-of-lading number a degenerate dimension and let consignor, shipper, transporters and consolidators be roles of one business entity dimension (p.235).

Travel services: share date, customer and itinerary/ticket/segment numbers across flight, hotel and car rental fact tables so stays interleave into a trip; hotel-stay grain is the entire stay (p.235).

terms.definition: an aircraft taking off at one airport and landing at another without any intermediate stops
the portion of a trip on a single aircraft; segments may have one or more legs; the line item on an airline ticket coupon; revenue and mileage credit is generated at the segment level
what the passenger asked for, from origin to destination, possibly with several segments; gives an accurate picture of customer demand
equivalent to the entire airline ticket or reservation confirmation number
a stop of more than four hours on the ticket
multiple foreign keys in a fact table linking to views of a single underlying physical dimension table
a single dimension combining attributes of otherwise separate small dimensions, similar to a junk dimension
one row per unique combination of frequent flyer elite tier, home airport and club membership status
supplemental dimension keyed by primary date key and country name holding holiday, season and workday attributes
date and time expressed relative to a standard such as headquarters or GMT, alongside the local clock-on-the-wall date and time
